articles.body:

Constitutional Court of BiH: Republika Srpska Can’t Ban the Insignia of the Army of RBiH
articles.summary: The challenged provision of Article 359b of the Criminal Code of Bosnia and Herzegovina (Official Gazette of Republika Srpska Nos
articles.body: At the session, the Constitutional Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina ruled that the provision of the Criminal Code of Republika Srpska, which criminalizes the display and glorification of the symbols, the flag and the insignia of the Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, is unconstitutional! Among other things, the Court confirmed that its insignia belong to the military heritage of the Armed Forces of BiH and that their use is grounded in valid state regulations. “In this case, the Constitutional Court decided on the requests of eleven members of the House of Representatives of the Parliamentary Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Denis Bećirović, at the time of submitting a request, Chairman of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and Denis Zvizdić, at the time of submitting a request, the First Deputy Chair of the House of Representatives of the Parliamentary Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina, for a review of the constitutionality of Article 359b of the Criminal Code of Republika Srpska. The challenged provision of Article 359b of the Criminal Code of Bosnia and Herzegovina (Official Gazette of Republika Srpska Nos. 64/17, 104/18 – Constitutional Court of RS Decision, 15/21, 89/21, http://www.ohr.int – High Representative Decision No. 12/23, ‘Official Gazette of Republika Srpska’ No. 73/23, ‘Official Gazette of BiH’ No. 9/24 – Constitutional Court of BiH Decision, ‘Official Gazette of Republika Srpska’ Nos. 105/24 – Constitutional Court of RS Decision, 19/25, 31/25, ‘Official Gazette of BiH’ No. 36/25 – Constitutional Court of BiH Decision, ‘Official Gazette of Republika Srpska’ Nos. 85/25 – Constitutional Court of RS Decision, 92/25 – Law on the Cessation of Validity of Laws, 25/26, and 78/26) criminalized the public display, showing, production, reproduction, or in any way putting into circulation of flags, symbols, insignia, greetings, or slogans that promote or glorify the Army of RBiH. The Constitutional Court concluded that the provision of Article 359 b of the Criminal Code of Republika Srpska is not in line with Articles I(2) and III(3)(b) of the Constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina. In its reasoning for the decision, the Constitutional Court, among other things, emphasized that the challenged provision is not aligned with the laws regarding the use of official symbols and insignia of the Army of RBiH. The regulations of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina regarding the appearance and the use of symbols and insignia of the Army of RBiH continue to apply on the territory of BiH based on the constitutional principle of continuity approved by Article I(1) of the Constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina, in conjunction with Article 2 of Annex II to the Constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The National Assembly has no jurisdiction to decide on the cessation of validity of legal acts of the institutions of RBiH, whose continuity is constitutionally recognized. The challenged provision is therefore not aligned with Article III (3)(b) of the Constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina, in light of the continuity of legal provisions, as it disrupts the normative hierarchy which the Constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina unequivocally established in Article III (3) (b) through the harmonization of legal regulations within the legal systems according to their hierarchy, in which state laws must be aligned with the decisions of the institutions of BiH. In addition to this, pursuant to the decisions of the institutions of BiH, the Army of RBiH is part of the Armed Forces of BiH with its military heritage and identity, along with recognizable insignia, the display of which constitutes a duty for the respective infantry regiments. Therefore, the challenged provision is not aligned with Article I(2) of the Constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina because it violates the decisions of the institutions of BiH requiring members of the regiment to wear their regimental insignia.”

Four soldiers, seven gunmen killed during drug cartel leader's arrest in Mexico
articles.summary: Four Mexican soldiers were killed in the armed confrontation in the municipality of Guasave
articles.body: Four Mexican soldiers and seven gunmen were killed during an operation to arrest Fausto Isidoro, leader of the Beltran Leyva criminal organization, in Mexico's Sinaloa state, APA reports, citing the country's Ministry of National Defense. According to the ministry, armed members of the criminal group resisted military personnel attempting to arrest the cartel leader, known as "Chapo Isidro." Four Mexican soldiers were killed in the armed confrontation in the municipality of Guasave. Seven gunmen were killed in return fire, while eight suspects were detained. Among those arrested were the group's leader Fausto Isidoro, his cousin and deputy Herman, known as "Serafin," and Jose, who was responsible for the organization's financial affairs. They were transported by military aircraft to Mexico City and handed over to the Specialized Prosecutor's Office for Organized Crime. The other five suspects were transferred to the prosecutor's office in Culiacan, Sinaloa state. During the operation, authorities seized a large-caliber Barrett rifle, 10 firearms of various calibers, a grenade launcher, two hand grenades, ammunition, tactical equipment, narcotics and cash. According to Mexico's Ministry of National Defense, no civilians were injured during the operation.

articles.title: Poland flags Russian disinformation over alleged Ukrainian attack in Kaliningrad Oblast
articles.summary: Numerous fake Russian disinformation messages surrounding reports of an alleged Ukrainian attack on Kaliningrad Oblast are being recorded in Poland
articles.body: Numerous fake Russian disinformation messages surrounding reports of an alleged Ukrainian attack on Kaliningrad Oblast are being recorded in Poland. Source: Polish radio station RMF24, as reported by European Pravda Details: Poland's Centre for Countering Disinformation is closely monitoring the media and social media, Deputy Minister of Digital Affairs Paweł Olszewski announced on 22 November. Olszewski cited examples of the disinformation messages. Among them, in particular, were reports claiming that: "German troops stationed in Poland are coordinating a Ukrainian attack on Królewiec Oblast [the Polish name for Kaliningrad Oblast]", as well as "Lithuanians and Poles are attacking Russia using Ukrainian missiles". Olszewski also cited examples of false reports claiming that "Ukrainians are attacking Russia to drag Poland into the war", and that "NATO has attacked Kaliningrad". "Remember to check reports against official information from the Polish authorities," Olszewski urged. Background: Overnight on 21-22 November, Lithuanian Foreign Minister Kęstutis Budrys said that Vilnius "categorically rejects false claims circulating on social media" regarding Lithuanian involvement in a drone attack on targets in Kaliningrad Oblast and had not granted permission for the use of its airspace for raids on facilities in Russia. According to the Telegram channel Exilenova+, activity by Russian air defence systems has been recorded in Baltiysk, Kaliningrad Oblast. The channel's authors suggest that the target of the attack was Baltiysk's port infrastructure. Early reports indicated that drones were heading in that direction earlier today in the morning – they were spotted over the Gulf of Finland, the channel claims. Local residents reported explosions in the port area. On Saturday 21 November, the Finnish defence forces detected a drone attack on a Russian merchant vessel west of Suursaari in international waters in the eastern Gulf of Finland. A Ukrainian expert said the drone had struck the Sparta II, which Russia has used for military operations – specifically to transport weapons from Syria for likely use in the war against Ukraine. Ruling party outlines grounds to impeach chief justice
articles.summary: Yonhap Supreme Court Chief Justice Cho Hee-dae arrives for work at the Supreme Court in Seocho District, Seoul, Friday
articles.body: Rep. Yang Bu-nam, center, who leads the ruling Democratic Party of Korea’s task force on impeaching Supreme Court Chief Justice Cho Hee-dae, speaks at a press briefing in the party leader’s office at the National Assembly, Sunday. Yonhap Supreme Court Chief Justice Cho Hee-dae arrives for work at the Supreme Court in Seocho District, Seoul, Friday. Yonhap The ruling Democratic Party of Korea (DPK) laid out its grounds Sunday for impeaching Supreme Court Chief Justice Cho Hee-dae and said it would seek a National Assembly vote by the end of December, drawing criticism that the move could undermine judicial independence. At its first public briefing at the Assembly, the party’s impeachment task force pointed to the Supreme Court’s handling of President Lee Jae Myung’s election law case and Cho’s refusal to recommend a new candidate for a vacant Supreme Court seat. “We will do our utmost to finalize the impeachment motion as quickly as possible and bring it to a vote in the National Assembly before the end of December,” said Rep. Yang Bu-nam, who leads the task force. He did not give a date for filing the motion. Other grounds previously raised by the party include the court’s response to the Dec. 3, 2024, martial law declaration, allegations over court operating expenses and cash payments, and Cho’s refusal to testify before the Assembly. The DPK made pursuing Cho’s impeachment its official position Friday, a day after the Supreme Court sent former Prime Minister Han Duck-soo’s insurrection case back to the Seoul High Court. The court found insufficient evidence that Han intended to subvert the constitutional order when he urged then-President Yoon Suk Yeol to convene a Cabinet meeting before the latter declared martial law. It upheld findings that some of Han’s actions after the declaration amounted to participation in the insurrection. Yang said the ruling had pushed the party’s patience to its limit. “We will not cite the substance of the ruling as a ground for impeachment,” he said. The task force will review allegations of serious procedural flaws in how the court heard the case, he added. The main opposition People Power Party (PPP) has called the impeachment push political retaliation. “Did the DPK decide to pursue impeachment first and only then look for grounds?” PPP chief spokesperson Rep. Choi Bo-yun said in a statement Sunday, accusing the DPK of deciding to pursue impeachment before establishing its grounds. She urged the ruling party to drop the effort, warning that impeaching Cho over a ruling backed by a majority of Supreme Court justices would undermine judicial independence. “It was a very emotional decision,” said Lee Jong-hoon, a political commentator and adviser at Daeryun Law Firm, referring to the DPK’s decision to pursue impeachment after the ruling in Han’s case. Lee said DPK leader Kim Min-seok had previously urged the party to hold a parliamentary inquiry first and give impeachment more thought. “I thought the Supreme Court got it right,” Lee said of the court’s judgment on Han’s actions before martial law was declared. Dispute over vacant seat The dispute over the vacant seat turns on whether the president can require the chief justice to recommend a different candidate. Under the Constitution, the president appoints Supreme Court justices on the chief justice’s recommendation and with the Assembly’s consent. The DPK argues that Cho’s refusal to put forward another candidate infringed on the president’s appointment power. In a statement opposing the DPK’s earlier push for a parliamentary inquiry into Cho, Kim Hyun, standing representative of People Making Good Laws, argued that the Constitution imposes no duty on the chief justice to consult the president in advance or recommend a replacement candidate. “Raising the prospect of an inquiry and impeachment over the exercise of a constitutional power amounts to political pressure on the chief justice to exercise his nominating authority in line with the president’s wishes,” Kim said. The rift between Lee and Cho dates back to the 2025 presidential campaign. On May 1, 2025, just over a month before the election, the Supreme Court’s full bench overturned an appeals court ruling that had acquitted Lee, then the DPK candidate, of violating the Public Official Election Act. It sent the case back to the Seoul High Court. The DPK accused the court of rushing the case to influence the vote. The court said it had reviewed the case swiftly and thoroughly in keeping with election law. The two clashed again in August, when Cho recommended Sohn Bong-ki, a senior judge at the Daegu District Court, for a Supreme Court seat. The presidential office declined to submit the nomination to the Assembly for confirmation and asked Cho to put forward another candidate. Cho rejected the request in September, saying the presidential office had failed to give a specific reason or identify a constitutional basis for it. The presidential office countered that his interpretation infringed on the president’s appointment power. Read More Why president, chief justice are clashing over Supreme Court seat

articles.title: Selling ‘success’ courses in Kazakhstan will soon require real credentials
articles.summary: Kazakhstan plans to require bloggers and coaches who offer online courses to disclose their educational qualifications
articles.body: Kazakhstan plans to require bloggers and coaches who offer online courses to disclose their educational qualifications. The proposed rules would also cover tarot readers, fortune-tellers and psychics . The amendments were approved at a Nov. 18 meeting of the Kurultai, Kazakhstan’s parliament. Bloggers who teach their audiences how to make money , run a business or master a profession will be required to disclose their educational qualifications. These credentials must be supported by relevant diplomas or certificates. The requirement would apply not only to paid online courses but also to other educational content published by creators on social media and online platforms. The amendments do not explicitly prohibit people without formal qualifications from selling courses. Instead, they require creators to disclose their relevant educational backgrounds. Specific penalties for failing to comply have not yet been established. The proposed regulations also cover tarot readers, fortune-tellers and psychics. The legislation introduces the term «occult services,» referring to services based on supernatural abilities or methods that lack scientific validation. Providers of such services will have to inform their audiences that the content is intended for entertainment purposes only and has no scientific or practical basis. For example, tarot readings and predictions about the future will have to carry an appropriate disclaimer. The amendments do not ban fortune-telling or other esoteric practices themselves. Another proposed measure concerns social media users with audiences exceeding 5,000 followers. The government agency responsible for overseeing the sector would be authorized to maintain a registry of these users. The draft legislation also proposes prohibiting children under 16 from registering on social media platforms. The new requirements are not yet in force. The amendments must still pass the remaining stages of the legislative process before they can take effect. The government has been considering tighter oversight of online education and coaching services for some time. In February 2026, Prime Minister Olzhas Bektenov announced plans to require bloggers to disclose information about their professional education. In May 2026, Yevgeniy Kochetov , who was then serving as deputy minister of culture and information, said the authorities were also discussing the creation of a unified registry of psychologists and coaches. The proposed registry would allow clients to check specialists’ educational credentials before paying for their services.

Ten people, including Russians and Libyans, suffered minor injuries after an alleged Ukrainian drone attack on a Russian warship in Libya.

The warship was hit as it was docked at the Benghazi naval base in eastern Libya, Libya's eastern-based government said.

Officials locally told Reuters they believed Ukraine was behind the attack. Kyiv has not yet commented.

In separate developments, a commercial vessel sailing under the Maltese flag was targeted by a naval drone in the same area this evening, military sources said.

Libyan naval forces rescued the crew members ⁠of the vessel, the sources added, as forces had to intercept more than 20 drones.

articles.title: Bahrain says Iranian strike wounds two, one critically
articles.summary: Iran's Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) has repeatedly said they targeted US facilities in Bahrain, where Iranian strikes resumed earlier in November
articles.body: Bahrain said on Sunday that two people were wounded in an Iranian strike the previous day on “a civilian industrial site” in the Gulf kingdom, which has faced several attacks this week. Iran's Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) has repeatedly said they targeted US facilities in Bahrain, where Iranian strikes resumed earlier in November. "In the wake of the criminal Iranian attacks suffered yesterday (Saturday) by the Kingdom of Bahrain… a Bahraini national with a disability was wounded," Bahrain's interior ministry said on X. "His condition is stable. A Pakistani resident was also wounded and is in critical condition." Residents had seen smoke rising above Sitra Island, east of Manama, which hosts several industrial facilities, including a refinery operated by the state-owned oil company Bapco, AFP reported. In a statement carried by Iranian state media on Saturday evening, the IRGC said they had attacked US Patriot air defence systems with missiles and drones at the Al-Riffa and Awali bases in Bahrain, in response to the “continued violations of the airspace” of the Islamic Republic. Bahrain's foreign ministry dismissed the IRGC's account, saying the site hit was purely civilian and industrial, calling the attack a direct danger to civilians and a violation of the kingdom's sovereignty. Bahrain's neighbour Saudi Arabia on Sunday also condemned Tehran for its attacks on Gulf countries. The Saudi foreign ministry expressed on X "the strongest condemnation and denunciation... of the criminal Iranian attacks against a civilian industrial facility in the brotherly Kingdom of Bahrain". As a result of the heinous Iranian attacks on Bahrain yesterday, a Bahraini citizen with disabilities sustained injuries and is in stable condition, while a Pakistani resident was also injured and is in critical condition. articles.title: Ukraine thought to be behind strike on Russian warship in Libya, officials say
articles.summary: It was a suspected Ukrainian drone strike that hit a Russian warship in Libya, officials have said
articles.body:
It was a suspected Ukrainian drone strike that hit a Russian warship in Libya, officials have said.

The strike at the Benghazi naval base in the country's east severely damaged the Merkury, a Russian Navy corvette, and ignited a fire at the facility, two Libyan military officials said.

At least four drones were intercepted and destroyed, while two hit the warship, they told Reuters.

The officials are affiliated with the self-styled Libyan National Army, which controls eastern and southern Libya.

Libya has been divided since a NATO-backed uprising toppled longtime dictator Muammar Gaddafi, who was later killed, in 2011. A UN-supported government is based in Tripoli and a rival administration in the east.

In a statement, the eastern Libya-based government said the Sunday strike caused an explosion and fire at the base, which was later extinguished.

The ship had docked at the base for refuelling and resupplying and a joint investigation was launched with Russia to "uncover the circumstances of the attack, its source, and the party behind it".

In March, Ukrainian forces operating in western Libya hit a Russian tanker in the Mediterranean in a suspected sea drone attack near Maltese waters, Libyan officials said at the time.

The Ukrainian forces, most of them drone experts, operated mainly at an air base in the coastal city of Misrata, but also at other military facilities in the capital, Tripoli, and the coastal town of Zawiya, the officials told The Associated Press.

articles.title: Germany tests kamikaze drones - as allies learn lessons from war in Ukraine
articles.summary: Germany's army began its first tactical tests of kamikaze drones in Lithuania today
articles.body:
Germany's army began its first tactical tests of kamikaze drones in Lithuania today.

They were undertaken as part of a wider joint drone exercise involving Ukraine, Germany, the US, Britain and Lithuania.

The tests mark a significant step for Germany, which made the decision to buy kamikaze drones - drones which explode on impact - in 2025, after years of controversy.

It also reflects the growing lessons Kyiv's allies are learning from Ukraine and its defence against Russia's invasion.

Both Russia and Ukraine utilise kamikaze drones extensively, with drone warfare being one of, if not the most, impactful fields of combat.

In Rudninkai...

At the Rudninkai training ground, near the Belarusian border, German army chief Christian Freuding watched kamikaze drones made by German companies plummet from the sky and strike targets.

articles.title: No deaths reported after Russian warship struck in 'drone attack'
articles.body:
We've got more details to bring you now on the Russian ship that was reportedly struck in a drone attack while at a Libyan port.

Naval News reports that the ship had been at the Benghazi naval base for several days before the attack.

It also provisionally identified the ship as a Project 20380 Steregushchiy-class corvette Merkury, which is worth about £150m.

Citing satellite images of the damaged ship, the outlet added that it had "almost certainly been destroyed".

'Settling scores'

Libya's eastern-based government said the ship had stopped at the port to refuel and resupply on its way back to Russia, under maritime agreements between the two countries.

Two medical sources told Reuters that ​no deaths had been reported, ⁠but there were injuries.

The ⁠number and nationalities of those injured are not known.

The Libyan government condemned the suspected attack, adding: "The Libyan government will not allow Libyan ports, territory or ⁠territorial waters to be turned ​into an arena for settling scores or ​exporting international conflicts."

articles.title: Russian cargo ship still on fire off Finland after attack
articles.body:
A fire onboard a Russian cargo ship ​that was struck by drones in the Baltic Sea continued to burn through the night even as efforts were made to douse the flames, Finland's coast guard said ⁠on Sunday.

The Finnish military has said the strike on the Sparta II on Saturday was likely carried out by Ukraine and that the vessel later drifted into Finnish waters where it remains at anchor. The ⁠16 crew members were evacuated onto ​a ⁠nearby Russian ship.

Pictures and video released by the coast guard showed several vessels spraying the Sparta II with ⁠water cannons during the night in a bid to put ​out ⁠the flames and cool down containers ‌stacked on its deck.

Ukraine has sent waves of military drones towards Russia's northwest coastal Leningrad region this year, including some that ‌strayed into the airspace of nearby Baltic ‌countries, leading to fears that the war was spilling onto NATO territory.

The ship, bound for Russian exclave Kaliningrad, was damaged in international waters west of Russia's ⁠Gogland island, Finland's Defence Forces have said, corroborating an account by Russian officials.

articles.title: Saudi Arabia, Qatar join condemnation of Iran attack on Bahrain
articles.summary: Saudi Arabia and Qatar have joined the UAE in condemning Iran's attack on Bahrain earlier on Sunday
articles.body: Saudi Arabia and Qatar have joined the UAE in condemning Iran's attack on Bahrain earlier on Sunday. In a statement posted on X, Qatar's foreign ministry expressed its "categorical rejection of attacks on economic facilities, civilian objects and civilians, and affirms that the continuation of these attacks represents a dangerous escalation that threatens the region’s security and stability”. Saudi Arabia, meanwhile, said it "affirms its full solidarity with Bahrain in all measures it takes to protect its security and stability", accusing Tehran of "undermining regional security and stability”. articles.title: Air alert sounds in Kaliningrad following drone strike in Gulf of Finland
articles.body:
A rare air alert sounded in Kaliningrad, the Russian exclave near Poland and Lithuania, according to the local governor, as claims circulated online of drone activity near a major naval base there.

The alert late Saturday in Kaliningrad came hours after a drone strike in the Gulf of Finland set fire to a Russian cargo ship bound for the region, which is a key base for Russia's Baltic Fleet. Finnish emergency services were still working to extinguish the blaze on Sunday.

Photos and video posted online show drone activity around the city of Baltiysk, where much of the fleet is stationed. But The Associated Press couldn't immediately verify the authenticity of the images.

According to local media, air raid sirens were heard in Kaliningrad for the first time since Russia’s all-out invasion of Ukraine on Feb. 24, 2022.

The Kaliningrad governor, Alexei Bezprozvannykh, said that “a suspicious object coming from the direction of Lithuania” triggered the alert in the Nemansky district near the Lithuanian border, about 170 kilometers (105 miles) northeast of Baltiysk.

The United Arab Emirates on Sunday condemned "in the strongest terms" the renewed attack by Iran on Bahrain.

On Saturday, Bahrain's interior ministry said Iran had attacked a civilian industrial facility, sparking a fire and causing material damage. No injuries were reported.

It marked the fourth attempted attack by Iran in Bahrain in roughly a week, a sharp escalation following a relative lull of attacks linked to Iran on U.S.-associated targets in the Gulf.

The UAE's foreign ministry said that Saturday's attack "constitutes a flagrant violation" of Bahrain's sovereignty and a "threat to its security and stability."

"The Ministry reiterated the UAE's full solidarity with the Kingdom of Bahrain and its support for all measures aimed at safeguarding its security and stability," the ministry said in a post on X.

editorialRejections.title: Strike on Kerch Bridge comparable in significance to hitting strategic target in Moscow – expert

editorialRejections.body: This opinion was expressed in a comment to Ukrinform by Lubomir Horak, a retired Lieutenant Colonel of the Czech Army, participant in international missions and military diplomat. The expert described the attacks on the Kerch Bridge as a major success for Ukrainian forces. According to Horak, the information released following the attacks about the units involved in the operation, its various stages and how long it had been planned undoubtedly confirms current planning, organizational and operational capabilities of the Ukrainian military. “For those unfamiliar with military affairs, this is roughly equivalent, from a military standpoint, to a situation in which Ukrainian forces managed to hit a strategic target in the very heart of Moscow. Moreover, it is widely known what the Kerch Bridge means to the Kremlin, both in terms of strategically supplying Crimea and its symbolic and propaganda significance,” the expert noted. He pointed out that, despite all its efforts, Russia had failed to protect the bridge and had learned no lessons from previous Ukrainian attacks in 2022, 2023 and 2025. Russia’s inability to protect this massive structure also points to weaknesses and current limitations in its air defense and military intelligence capabilities, as well as shortcomings in the security of strategic facilities and coordination among individual security agencies, Horak stressed. According to him, this also calls into question the ability of the Russian command to properly assess and anticipate potential threats, take effective preventive measures and learn from its units’ previous failures. “And that is undoubtedly good news,” the expert added. At the same time, he emphasized that such a complex operation, like the previous ones, required considerable courage, immense determination and heroism from those directly involved. “Almost five years into the full-scale war in Ukraine, there are still many soldiers and service members who risk their lives for their homeland every day. Such soldiers are the most valuable asset any army has. Thanks to them, not only battles but also wars have been won throughout history. When soldiers fight for a country that has been attacked, for their families, for freedom and against evil in its purest form, they are not only determined and motivated but also strong, and often superhumanly brave. That is why those who have fought with such a mindset in the past have been able to defeat even better-equipped and numerically superior enemies,” Horak said. He also quoted a battle motto attributed to Czech historical hero Jan Žižka and the Hussites, which is also associated with Czechoslovak pilots of the Royal Air Force's No. 311 (Czechoslovak) Bomber Squadron: “Do not fear the enemy, do not count their numbers.” Horak congratulated the Armed Forces of Ukraine on their upcoming professional holiday on December 6, as well as all military personnel, both those serving in the trenches and those in command positions. “They are the most valuable asset any army has, and even the most advanced and expensive equipment cannot replace them,” the Czech military diplomat stressed. He wished Ukraine’s defenders not only courage and bravery in battle but also “common sense, sufficient humility and humanity, and a great deal of good luck.” Above all, he wished them a safe return to their families after the war and expressed hope that politicians would speed up that return through their decisions. “And last but not least, may the sacrifices of those who will never return home never be considered in vain,” Horak added. Lubomir Horak is a former professional service member and Lieutenant Colonel who took part in international missions in Bosnia and Herzegovina, Kosovo and Afghanistan and later served as a military diplomat. He supports Ukraine, including through participation in RUN4UKR, a charity project supporting the Ukrainian Armed Forces. As Ukrinform reported, Russia currently lacks the necessary technical conditions to repair the Kerch Bridge. Alternative routes to temporarily occupied Crimea remain the land corridor through the occupied territories of the Azov region and ferry crossings.

editorialRejections.title: Ukraine's Defence Forces strike eight Russian oil infrastructure facilities in one week
editorialRejections.summary: Ukrainian forces attacked facilities essential to fuel production and supply, military transportation, drone operations, strategic infrastructure protection, and equipment maintenance
editorialRejections.reason: Ukraine coverage requires an international news source
editorialRejections.body: The ministry noted that the period was marked not by a single high-profile strike, but by sustained operations targeting various components of Russia's military system. Ukrainian forces attacked facilities essential to fuel production and supply, military transportation, drone operations, strategic infrastructure protection, and equipment maintenance. One of the main areas of Ukrainian operations was the systematic targeting of Russia's oil infrastructure. During the night of November 16, Ukraine's Defence Forces attacked the Ilsky Oil Refinery in Russia's Krasnodar Krai. The strikes hit the AT-4, AT-5, and AT-6 primary oil-processing units, as well as the facility's motor gasoline production complex. The refinery has an annual processing capacity of approximately 6.6 million tonnes of oil. Its geographical location makes it important for supplying Russian forces operating in the southern direction and in temporarily occupied Crimea. Ukrainian drones also attacked Russia's Rostov region. Fires broke out at four industrial facilities in the city of Azov. That same day, Ukraine's Defence Forces struck three oil depots in Azov, Rostov region: Flash Energy, Transit-Express, and Azovskaya. These facilities perform different functions within the fuel supply chain: Thus, the attacks targeted not only fuel production facilities but also infrastructure used to store, distribute, and deliver petroleum products to consumers. During the following night, November 17, Ukrainian forces struck the Gazprom Neftekhim Salavat petrochemical complex in Russia's Republic of Bashkortostan. The facility is located approximately 1,500 kilometres from the Ukrainian border and has an oil-processing capacity of around 10 million tonnes annually. It produces gasoline, diesel and aviation fuel, lubricants, and petrochemical products. Explosions were heard and a fire broke out at the complex following the strike. Also on November 17, operators of Ukraine's 1st Separate Unmanned Systems Center reported striking the Bashneft-Ufaneftekhim refinery in Ufa. The facility is part of the Ufa oil-refining complex, which has a combined processing capacity of approximately 23.5 million tonnes of oil annually. During the night of November 18, Ukrainian forces struck the Ilsky refinery again and also attacked the Afipsky Oil Refinery in Krasnodar Krai. According to the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, the tank farm at the Ilsky refinery was hit, while an oil-processing unit was struck at the Afipsky refinery. The extent of the damage at Ilsky was subsequently clarified: one RVS-5000 storage tank was destroyed, while eight other tanks of various capacities were damaged. A section of the oil pipeline, technical buildings, and a warehouse building were also damaged. Another significant operation took place on November 19, when Ukrainian forces struck the Kaleykino oil pumping station near Almetyevsk in Russia's Republic of Tatarstan. This is one of the key facilities in Russia's oil transportation system. It receives and blends oil from different regions before directing it to refineries and into the Druzhba main oil pipeline system. According to the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, three RVSPA-50,000 storage tanks at the Kaleykino-1 oil pumping station were confirmed hit. One tank caught fire, while two others were damaged. Each tank has a storage capacity of up to 50,000 cubic metres of oil. The significance of this strike extends beyond local infrastructure. The facility is a major hub connecting oil production, refining, and subsequent transportation. Disrupting such facilities creates additional difficulties for the operation of the entire oil supply chain. Another important area of operations involved transportation infrastructure used by the Russian military to supply its occupation forces. During the night of November 16, Ukraine's Defence Forces struck the Kerch Bridge, which connects temporarily occupied Crimea with mainland Russia. Following the attack, traffic across the bridge was temporarily suspended, and damage to its structures and roadway was reported. The attack continued during the night of November 17, when the collapse of a road arch was reported. This incident demonstrated how difficult it is for Russia to guarantee the security of even infrastructure it has spent years portraying as heavily protected. Another strike against the Kerch Bridge took place during the night of November 19. This time, Ukraine's Missile Forces, in coordination with other components of the Defence Forces, used Neptune coastal missile systems operated by the Ukrainian Navy. According to the General Staff, the target was hit, traffic across the bridge was suspended, and the railway tracks were damaged. The military significance of these strikes is primarily linked to the bridge's role as a major transportation artery used by Russia to deliver fuel, ammunition, weapons, and military equipment to occupied Crimea and further toward the southern front. “The Kerch Bridge is not the only supply route for Russian forces. However, disruptions to its operation increase the burden on alternative routes, complicate transportation planning, and create additional logistical constraints,” the Ministry of Defence emphasized. These operations complemented earlier strikes against river crossings. Essentially, Ukraine's forces are systematically creating obstacles along routes used by the Russian military to move personnel, fuel, ammunition, and equipment. Operations against Russian air defence systems, electronic warfare equipment, and military command infrastructure were equally important. On November 17, the General Staff reported strikes against ten Russian radar systems and electronic warfare stations. In particular, two electronic warfare stations were hit: one near Yakovenkove in temporarily occupied Crimea and another near Pryazovske in Krasnodar Krai. These facilities are important components of Russia's system for detecting, tracking, and countering Ukrainian drones. Disabling them can reduce the enemy's ability to detect aerial targets in time and interfere with their operations. On November 19 and during the night of November 20, Ukraine's Defence Forces continued targeting Russian military infrastructure. In Russia's Bryansk region, Ukrainian forces struck a Pantsir-S2 air defence missile and gun system. The system is designed to protect military and infrastructure facilities against aerial threats, including drones and missiles. Near Selydove in Donetsk region, Ukrainian forces struck a Russian military drone command post. Such centres coordinate drone operators, flight operations, and the deployment of UAVs against Ukrainian positions and settlements. In addition, Russian military supply depots were struck near Rubizhne and Lysychansk in Luhansk region. Near Berdiansk in Zaporizhzhia region, Ukrainian forces hit a site where weapons and military equipment were concentrated. Another important result was announced by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky on November 20. He reported that Ukraine's Defence Forces had struck three launchers belonging to Russian missile systems designed to fire ballistic weapons during a single night. At the time of the announcement, the destruction of one target had been confirmed, while the results concerning the other two were still being assessed. “This is particularly important given that Russia continues to use ballistic missiles to attack Ukrainian cities, energy infrastructure, and civilian facilities. Detecting and striking missile launchers directly affects the enemy's ability to prepare and carry out such attacks,” the ministry noted. During the night of November 21, Ukraine's Defence Forces also struck an ammunition depot belonging to a Russian military unit near Pervomaiske in temporarily occupied Crimea. Command posts belonging to Russian military units were hit near Pryshyb in Zaporizhzhia region and Ukrainsk in Donetsk region. These targets form part of a broader picture: Ukrainian forces are not only attacking Russian weapons systems but also undermining the enemy's ability to command troops, accumulate resources, and coordinate military operations. During the night of November 18, Ukrainian forces struck a Russian military repair base near Khomutovka in Russia's Kursk region. Such facilities are responsible for repairing damaged armoured vehicles, cars, and other military equipment. When Russia loses repair capacity, it loses not only a particular facility but also the ability to quickly return damaged equipment to service. This increases the workload on other repair units and complicates the supply of operational equipment to frontline forces. On November 18, the General Staff also reported the results of a strike against Russia's 123rd Aircraft Repair Plant in Staraya Russa, Novgorod region. The attack had actually taken place on November 10, but its consequences were clarified later. According to confirmed information, three Russian Aerospace Forces military transport aircraft were damaged, including a heavy Il-76 aircraft. This is significant because military transport aviation plays an important role in moving personnel, equipment, cargo, and other resources over long distances. Damage to aircraft and repair infrastructure limits Russia's ability to restore its aviation equipment and keep it operational. The defining feature of Ukraine's operations during this period was their comprehensive impact on Russia's military machine. War is not limited to direct clashes between military units along the frontline. To continue offensive operations, the Russian military needs fuel, ammunition, functioning equipment, secure supply routes, communications, intelligence, and command systems. It also requires air defence systems to protect military facilities and rear-area infrastructure. These interconnected elements have all come under pressure from Ukrainian strikes. Strikes against refineries, oil depots, and pumping stations create problems at different stages of the fuel cycle, from production to storage and transportation. This can complicate the supply of Russian military forces while also affecting the economic resources used to finance the war. Strikes against the Kerch Bridge and other crossings force Russia to seek alternative routes, change transportation arrangements, and spend more time delivering supplies. For an army operating across a vast territory, even additional logistical difficulties can have significant consequences. Strikes against air defence systems, radar installations, and electronic warfare stations create gaps in Russia's protective infrastructure. This matters not only for individual attacks but also for future operations involving Ukrainian drone and missile systems. Drone command posts, warehouses, and sites where military equipment and weapons are concentrated are important components of combat support. Striking these facilities can disrupt coordination, reduce available resources, and complicate preparations for offensive operations. Attacks against repair bases, aircraft repair facilities, and military transport aviation affect how quickly Russia can compensate for losses, return equipment to service, and move resources. Damage to fuel infrastructure affects logistics. Disrupted logistics complicate the supply of military units. Weakened air defence creates additional opportunities for subsequent strikes. Meanwhile, the destruction of repair and command capabilities makes it more difficult for Russia to restore its military system after suffering losses. The events of November 16–21 demonstrate that Ukraine's Defence Forces continue to target not only direct military objectives but also the infrastructure that enables Russia to wage war. From oil refineries in Krasnodar Krai and Bashkortostan to an oil pumping station in Tatarstan, from the Kerch Bridge to ammunition depots, command posts, air defence systems, and repair facilities, Ukrainian strikes have affected multiple levels of Russia's military system. This does not mean that every strike automatically shuts down a facility or prevents the Russian military from carrying out a particular task. The extent of damage and the time required for repairs vary from one target to another. However, the cumulative effect of these operations is that Russia must devote more resources to protection, restoration, logistical adjustments, and compensating for its losses. Ukraine's strategy is not limited to destroying Russian military assets directly on the battlefield. It also seeks to systematically deprive the Russian military of the resources, routes, and capabilities that allow it to continue fighting. As Ukrinform previously reported, during the night of November 22, drones reportedly struck the Main Directorate of Russia's National Guard (Rosgvardiya) in Krasnodar Krai , where a fire may have broken out, according to media reports.

editorialRejections.title: Saida Mirziyoyeva visits US aircraft carrier near India
editorialRejections.summary: Photographs of the visit appeared on the carrier’s Instagram account on 20 November
editorialRejections.reason: US coverage requires an international or US news source
editorialRejections.body: Tashkent, Uzbekistan (UzDaily.uz) — Saida Mirziyoyeva, head of Uzbekistan’s Presidential Administration, visited the US nuclear-powered aircraft carrier USS George Washington off the coast of India, she said on her Telegram channel on 22 November. Photographs of the visit appeared on the carrier’s Instagram account on 20 November. Mirziyoyeva was welcomed aboard by the US ambassador to India and US President Donald Trump’s special envoy for South and Central Asia, Sergio Gor. Mirziyoyeva and Gor are co-chairs of the American-Uzbek Business and Investment Council. "It was interesting to see how this huge ship is organised, learn about its remarkable technologies and get a glimpse of the crew’s daily life," Mirziyoyeva wrote. Guests, including representatives of other countries, were given a demonstration of the nuclear-powered carrier’s capabilities and US naval aviation. The USS George Washington is named after the first US president. The ship was launched on 21 July 1990. It is 333 metres long and 76.8 metres wide, with a flight deck covering 18,000 square metres. The carrier can accommodate around 90 aircraft and helicopters.

editorialRejections.title: Kazakhstan enters top UN e-government ranking tier for first time
editorialRejections.summary: The tier comprises 21 countries with the most advanced e-government systems
editorialRejections.reason: Local outlet reports an event outside its home country without a local subject
editorialRejections.body: Tashkent, Uzbekistan (UzDaily.uz) — Kazakhstan has risen from 24th to 16th place among 193 countries in the United Nations E-Government Development Index (UN EGDI), entering its highest rating tier, VH, for the first time. The tier comprises 21 countries with the most advanced e-government systems. Kazakhstan is now grouped with South Korea, Denmark, Singapore, the United Kingdom, Estonia and the United States. Kazakhstan’s index score increased from 0.9009 to 0.9363 over two years, compared with a global average of 0.6675. The country recorded one of the strongest growth rates among the ranking’s leading countries, outperforming Germany, Sweden and Japan. Kazakhstan also retained its first place among CIS and Central Asian countries. The UN highlighted progress in several areas, including telecommunications infrastructure, internet access, public digital literacy and the quality of online government services. The eGov.kz and eGov Mobile platforms were cited in the report as examples of an integrated digital government. The results reflect Kazakhstan’s strengthening position in the digitalisation of public administration.

editorialRejections.title: Explosion on Russian ship at Libya port caused by suspected drone attack, officials say
editorialRejections.summary: It added that the site was secured, and there were no casualties
editorialRejections.body: Satellite imagery showed a ship on fire at the port early on Sunday morning An explosion on a Russian ship docked at Benghazi naval base port was caused by a suspected drone attack, Libya's eastern government has said. The explosion happened at dawn on Sunday, while the ship had stopped for fuel and supplies on its way back to Russia, Libyan state media reported, citing the eastern government. It added that the site was secured, and there were no casualties. Moscow has yet to comment. Satellite imagery from Planet Labs PBC, reviewed by BBC Verify, shows a boat on fire at 0547 GMT at the Benghazi port, with a separate image captured several hours later appearing to show the same vessel partially submerged. Videos posted on social media and geolocated by BBC Verify show the ship engulfed in flames and smoke, while it is still dark. The eastern-based Government of National Stability (GNS) said the Russian ship was using the Benghazi port within the framework of an existing maritime agreement. Sunday's incident is under investigation, and authorities are coordinating with their Russian counterparts to determine the source of the suspected attack and who is responsible for it, GNS added. GNS condemned the attack on a ship inside a Libyan port, and called it a violation of maritime safety and an attack on their sovereignty. It said Libya was not party to the Russia-Ukraine war, or any other conflict beyond its borders. Separately, Libya's internationally recognised government in Tripoli - the Government of National Unity (GNU) - warned against hosting foreign forces and allowing them to use facilities in a statement published by state media. GNU said such activity raises "serious fears" about "risks that may result from involving ports and civilian facilities in activities related to external conflicts, and the resulting threat to the lives of citizens and the safety of national facilities and assets". Libya fractured into violence and instability after its leader Muammar Gaddafi was overthrown in 2011, leading to the opposing governments. Benghazi is more than 2,000 km (1,243 miles) away from the Russian capital Moscow. Three West African juntas have turned to Russia. editorialRejections.title: Russian ship hit in Benghazi by suspected Ukrainian drone attack, say Libyan officials
editorialRejections.summary: The strike severely damaged the Merkury, a Russian navy warship, and ignited a fire at the naval base, they said
editorialRejections.body: A suspected Ukrainian drone attack caused an explosion on a Russian warship docked at the naval base in the Libyan port city of Benghazi, Libyan officials have said. The strike severely damaged the Merkury, a Russian navy warship, and ignited a fire at the naval base, they said. Several Ukrainian sea drones were launched at the ship from a base run by Ukrainian forces in western Libya , according to an initial investigation into the attack. At least four drones were intercepted and destroyed, while two hit the warship, the officials told the Associated Press. The officials were affiliated with the self-styled Libyan National Army, which controls eastern and southern Libya. There was no immediate reaction from Russian authorities, and no immediate claim of responsibility for the strike, but it comes as Ukrainian forces have stepped up their long-range barrages against Russia far beyond the frontlines. Authorities in divided Libya’s east said in a statement that the vessel had stopped at Benghazi port to refuel and ⁠resupply on its way back to Russia, ​under maritime cooperation agreements between ‌the two ‌countries. Two medical sources told Reuters no deaths had been reported, but there were injuries. The ⁠number and nationalities of those injured are not yet known. In a separate attack, another sea drone hit a commercial vessel off the port of Benghazi on Sunday evening, Libyan military sources told Reuters. The ‌eastern-based Libyan authority said port and naval base facilities, including warehouses, were safe and that ​normal operations would resume once the fire was brought under control and the site secured. It condemned the suspected attack as a violation of Libya’s sovereignty and ⁠a threat to maritime safety, saying it would take ​legal and ​diplomatic measures against ​anyone found responsible. “The Libyan government will not ​allow Libyan ‌ports, territory or territorial ​waters ​to be turned into an arena for settling scores or exporting international conflicts,” it said. The specialist website Naval News also identified the ship attacked as the Merkury, a Russian corvette – the smallest class of warship, smaller than a frigate – and said it was almost certainly destroyed. HI Sutton, a naval analyst, said the attack was probably conducted by sea drones, after a photograph of one emerged apparently taken off the Libyan coast. The drone, he said, “is also likely the type used in the subsequent attack”. If it is confirmed that Ukraine has been able to blow up or seriously damage a Russian warship in Benghazi, it would represent one of its most successful naval strikes during the almost five-year war. But it also represents a risky extension of the fighting far beyond eastern Europe, in an incident that could affect civilians in another continent and the working of the port. A small unit of Ukrainian special forces operatives has been based at Misrata, western Libya, and is believed to have coordinated drone attacks on Russian tankers and transport ships in the past year. Initial reports and footage suggest the Merkury was struck from above, potentially by a drone, launched no more than a few kilometres away from the target in port. Russia is close to the Benghazi authorities that control eastern Libya. It uses the port, which has a growing importance since it lost bases in Syria, to supply Russian mercenary forces in Africa and as a base in the Mediterranean. Separately, a fire onboard a Russian cargo ship that was ⁠struck by drones in the ⁠Baltic Sea continued to smoulder ​on Sunday, Finland’s border guard said, with emergency services from Finland, Russia and Estonia working together to put out the blaze. The Finnish military said the strike on the Sparta II ⁠on Saturday was probably carried out by Ukraine and that the vessel later drifted into Finnish waters, where it remained at anchor. The 16 crew members were evacuated on to a nearby Russian ship. One crew member was slightly ⁠injured. On Sunday, visible flames had been put out, with operations focusing on cooling down the containers and stabilising the vessel, Finnish authorities said. The ship, bound for the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad, had been damaged in international waters west of Russia’s Gogland Island, Finland’s defence forces said, corroborating an account by Russian officials. Kyiv has sent waves of military drones towards the Leningrad region on Russia’s north-west coast this year, including some that strayed into the airspace of nearby Baltic countries, leading to fears that the war was spilling on to Nato territory. The risk of ⁠further attacks in the Gulf of Finland, a narrow arm of the Baltic Sea, could not be ruled ​out, Ivo Värk, the Estonian navy commander, told the public ​broadcaster ERR on Sunday. Finland’s military said last ​week it had detected a strike on a Russian warship in the same area during Ukrainian drone attacks.

editorialRejections.title: Suspected Ukrainian drone strike hits Russian warship at Libyan base
editorialRejections.body:
A suspected Ukrainian drone strike hit a Russian warship Sunday at a Libyan naval base, Libyan officials said, the latest attack in the North African nation linked to the Russia-Ukraine war.

The strike at the Benghazi Naval Base in eastern Libya severely damaged the Merkury, a Russian Navy corvette, and ignited a fire at the facility, two Libyan military officials said.

They said several Ukrainian sea drones were launched at the ship from a base run by Ukrainian forces in western Libya, according to an initial investigation into the attack. At least four drones were intercepted and destroyed, while two hit the warship, they said.

The officials, affiliated with the self-styled Libyan National Army, which controls eastern and southern Libya, spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not allowed to talk to reporters.

Libya has been divided since a NATO-backed uprising toppled longtime dictator Moammar Gadhafi, who was later killed, in 2011. A UN-supported government is based in Tripoli and a rival administration in the east. The oil-rich nation remains a focal point for a long-running rivalry between Russia and the West.

A Russian cargo ship that was reportedly attacked by drones remains on fire in the Gulf of Finland.

Finland's Border Guard said rescue operations for the Sparta II were ongoing this morning after it caught on fire and drifted into Finnish territorial waters.

The force said it wasn't aware of any danger to the surrounding maritime traffic.

Russian officials said drones had struck the ship, which is subject to US sanctions, while Finnish officials said it was likely Ukraine carried out the strike.

Several vessels were pictured spraying the Sparta II with water cannons overnight in attempts to put out flames ⁠and cool down containers stacked on ⁠its deck.
